parts.label: Part 4
parts.article:
We all think we know what makes children laugh, but can we really explain it? And is it useful for educators to be aware of how children’s humour works? Well, to answer these questions, I’d like to tell you about the large-scale study on the humour of primary school children that I was commissioned to carry out two years ago.

The aim of the study was to find out what children find funny in their everyday lives, both at school and at home. We wanted to know how children used humour to interact with each other. For example, when they were in the playground, we wanted to know what sort of jokes they told one another, and which ones were most popular. Some research was done in this area about fifty years ago, but it’s never been followed up. So that’s one area that we wanted to find out more about in our research. And we also wanted to find out about what children find funny when they’re at home watching television, since many children spend quite a significant amount of time doing this.

So how did we go about finding out this information? Well, we interviewed a total of 150 children in six different primary schools around the city. We had originally intended to have one-to-one interviews, but we decided that this would be too time-consuming, and also might be stressful for the children. So instead, each interviewer had several groups, each consisting of three or four children. They were asked questions like, what’s the thing that made you laugh? And do you know any funny stories? Then another method we used to collect information about what makes children laugh was through the use of humour diaries. So we asked the parents of some of the children to keep a diary like this for six months and to describe situations in which their children had laughed.

So what were the main findings? Well, some of them weren’t quite what you’d have expected. You’d think that people laugh when things are funny, but that’s not always the case. One thing we found is that children nearly always laugh if they’re in a situation which is unfamiliar to them. They’re a bit nervous because they’re not sure what sort of action it’s appropriate for them to take, so they laugh. The type of situation in which we found children often laughed was when people did things which were surprising. If someone’s walking down the street with a dog on a lead, that’s quite unsurprising, but if someone’s got a chicken on a lead, the child will laugh because the social conventions that govern our behaviour aren’t being followed. It’s funny because it’s surprising.

Another interesting area is what sort of person makes children laugh most. And here we found that nearly all primary school children find situations particularly humorous if they involve people looking foolish, and particularly if these are adults. The children probably find this empowering, to see them at a disadvantage for once. One thing that was observed frequently in the humour diaries was that laughter often erupted spontaneously during pretend games and role play. Our research showed there’s a strong link between laughter and being creative. It’s an area that’s received little attention to date, maybe because this type of humour isn’t often observed in research situations.

As well as these, there were other findings that we made during the research process. One quite surprising finding was the fact that when looking at what children find funny, there seems to be hardly any difference between boys and girls, so the children’s gender doesn’t seem to be significant. Boys sometimes show a slight preference for physical humour, but there’s nothing much in it. For educators, as well as for those involved in children’s media, it’s worth stressing that children still find many of the same things funny as they did in the past. There hasn’t been much change in what they laugh at over the years. If you look at what makes children laugh in the 21st century, there’s really not much difference from what made their grandparents laugh in the 20th century.

They still react positively to the same sort of things. So, for example, in the media, they enjoy humour which is non-verbal, where the humour comes from pictures rather than words. And one of the most striking findings that came out of our research, both the interviews and the diaries, is that just as in their grandparents’ generation, what children find incredibly funny is humour that is founded on some kind of danger. The fact that they know it isn’t real gives them permission to laugh somehow. So what we can conclude from all this is that humour is incredibly important to children. It plays a crucial role.

analyses.content: 题目问的是在操场上说的 "...types of 31..."，录音中明确提到想知道他们在操场上（playground）互相讲什么样的 "jokes"（笑话）。
For example, when they were in the playground, we wanted to know what sort of jokes they told one another, and which ones were most popular.
注意题目中的 "types of" 暗示后面接名词复数，且录音中 "sort of jokes" 的 "s" 听得比较清楚，不要漏写复数。
So instead, each interviewer had several groups, each consisting of three or four children.
不要填数字 "three" 或 "four"，也不要填 "primary schools"（这是大地点），这里填的是采访的形式单位“小组”。
题目说是在“小的（small）...”里进行采访，录音中说不是一对一，而是每个采访者负责几个 "groups"（小组），每组由三四个孩子组成。
So we asked the parents of some of the children to keep a diary like this for six months and to describe situations in which their children had laughed.
虽然日记内容是关于孩子的，但记日记的人是 "parents"，不要想当然地填了 "children" 或 "teachers"。
题目是被动语态 "kept by..."（由谁记录），录音中说是 "asked the parents... to keep a diary"（让父母记日记），执行者是父母。
They're a bit nervous because they're not sure what sort of action it's appropriate for them to take, so they laugh.
听到 "what sort of" 后面紧跟的就是答案，不要因为前面的 "nervous" 或后面的 "appropriate" 分心，固定搭配 "take action" 是关键。
题目是 "don't know what... to take"，录音中对应的是 "not sure what sort of... to take"，中间的核心词就是 "action"（行动）。

Another interesting area is what sort of person makes children laugh most. And here we found that nearly all primary school children find situations particularly humorous if they involve people looking foolish, and particularly if those are adults.
注意听清是指谁看起来愚蠢（look foolish），录音里强调的是如果是“大人”出丑，孩子会觉得更好笑，不要填成 "people"。
题目中的 "especially"（尤其）对应录音中的 "particularly"，紧随其后的对象就是 "adults"（成年人）。
题目是 "opportunity to be..."（成为...的机会），录音中提到笑与 "being creative"（有创造力）之间有很强的联系，词性形容词对应准确。
Our research showed there's a strong link between laughter and being creative.
题目是 "be" 后面接形容词，不要填成名词 "creativity"；另外 "spontaneously" 是副词修饰前面的动作，不是答案。

One quite surprising finding was the fact that when looking at what children find funny, there seems to be hardly any difference between boys and girls, so the children's gender doesn't seem to be significant.
虽然录音中提到了 "boys and girls"，但要归纳出这两个词的上义词 "gender"，且听到 "significant"（重要的）前面的否定表达。
题目说 "depends very little on..."（很少取决于），录音中说男孩女孩之间 "hardly any difference"，因此 "gender"（性别）不重要。
There hasn't been much change in what they laugh at over the years.
不要被下一句提到的 "20th century" 或 "grandparents" 干扰，这里强调的是随时间推移的“变化”很少。
题目是 "little... in children's humour"（几乎没有...），录音中对应 "not been much change"（没有太多改变），直接填名词。
So, for example, in the media, they enjoy humour which is non-verbal, where the humour comes from pictures rather than words.
前面提到的 "non-verbal"（非语言的）是形容词，题目空格在介词 "in" 之后，需要一个名词，"pictures" 更合适。
题目是 "shown in..."，录音中解释说幽默来自于 "pictures rather than words"（图片而不是文字），"pictures" 即为答案。

The fact that they know it isn't real gives them permission to laugh somehow. So what we can conclude from all this is that humour is incredibly important to children. It plays a crucial role... (Wait, looking at the previous sentence for the answer) ...And one of the most striking findings that came out of our research... is that just as in their grandparents' generation, what children find incredibly funny is humour that is founded on some kind of danger.
录音中先说了 "isn't real"（不真实），然后才引出 "founded on some kind of danger"，注意语序，不要填 "unreal"。
题目是 "based on..."，录音中对应 "founded on..."（建立在...之上），后面的核心词是 "danger"（危险）。
